extracted.intended_audience: experimental chemists / laboratory practitioners performing combustion and gasometry experiments
extracted.subtask_description: Practical laboratory procedures and apparatus design for sealing vessels, conducting controlled combustion (phosphorus, charcoal, oils, alcohol), and accurately collecting/measuring gaseous and condensed combustion products.

rubrics_metrics.name: Use of appropriate luts (seals) for glass apparatus
rubrics_metrics.description: Choice of sealing material: cires (wax) & resins work but soften with heat; 'lut gras' (clay + cooked linseed oil or vernis gras au succin) resists heat better and adheres to glass/metal/porcelain when surfaces are thoroughly dried.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Recipes and trade-offs: one pound of wax with 1.5–2 oz turpentine yields flexible lut that adheres well but melts with heat; lut gras prepared from fine dry clay beaten with cooked linseed oil (or vernis gras) gives superior tenacity and heat resistance but is more expensive. Ensure all joint surfaces are well dried before applying lut.

rubrics_metrics.name: Preparation and conditioning of lut gras
rubrics_metrics.description: Make lut gras by finely powdered, very-dry unbaked clay, passed through silk, pounded in an iron mortar while gradually adding cooked (oxygenated/siccative) linseed oil or vernis gras au succin.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Pounding for several hours with heavy pestle produces a tenacious lut; vernis gras (succin dissolved in oil) improves adherence but raises cost. Adjust consistency by resin addition to make it harder/softer as needed.

rubrics_metrics.name: Limitations and failure modes of luts
rubrics_metrics.description: Even good luts soften and may flow under considerable heat; moisture penetration between glass and lut makes re-sealing very difficult; heat can liquefy resin-based luts causing leaks.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Main inconvenience of lut gras: if humidity enters between glass and lut layers during operations, it's extremely hard to reclose openings. Cover lut with restraining bandages to prevent flow at elevated temperatures.

rubrics_metrics.name: Mechanical reinforcement of luts
rubrics_metrics.description: After applying lut, cover with bladder bands tightly wound and tied, or with linen strips soaked in egg-white and lime (or strong glue in water), then dried and tightened with coarse wire turns.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Procedure: moisten/twist bladder bands around lut, make ligatures above and below, then wind many turns of wire over the bladder; for shapes that cannot be ligatured (e.g., three-neck bottles), use linen strips with egg-white+lime to harden in place. Take care not to disturb adjacent vessels when tightening.

rubrics_metrics.name: Proper seating and alignment of joints before lutting
rubrics_metrics.description: Vessels must be firmly set and immobilized before sealing so parts cannot move; if necks have slight play, insert short matches or cork pieces to take up slack; for large mismatch use a precisely fitting cork with a drilled hole.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Ensure no movement can occur during lutting; otherwise tightening will disturb apparatus and ruin seals. For bent tubes to be sealed in bottle mouths, choose a cork drilled with appropriate hole sizes (single or multiple) and use a queue-de-rat file to make holes as needed.

rubrics_metrics.name: Method of applying lut and layering
rubrics_metrics.description: Soften (knead/heat slightly) the lut, roll into small cylinders, apply and press/flatten onto glass so it adheres, then add overlapping layers so each new layer overlaps the previous edge.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Work quickly yet accurately; inexperienced operators often must redo seals repeatedly, while practiced hands succeed first time. After forming the lut, cover with bladder or linen strips as described and avoid jostling the apparatus while tightening.

rubrics_metrics.name: Testing seals before beginning experiment
rubrics_metrics.description: Always test luts by lightly heating a flask or by blowing air through some tubes; pressure/pressure changes should displace liquid levels in connected tubes and remain displaced if the apparatus is well sealed.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: E.g., heat the cornue slightly or blow air through specified tubes ss's''s''' to observe liquid level changes; if liquid returns to original level the apparatus leaks. Never start an experiment without having tested the seals.

rubrics_metrics.name: Avoiding luts: mercury-sealed designs
rubrics_metrics.description: Where possible substitute lut by mercury-filled collars or hermetically jointed glass-to-glass fittings: double-gouleau bottles with an external trough (rigole) filled with mercury and a fitted glass lid produce hermetic closure without lut.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Design: inner and outer collars form a deep groove for mercury into which a glass cover adjusts; tubes are contoured to pass under cover and rise through the inner collar so the system communicates only via tubes. Suitable only when mercury is not attacked by distilled materials.

rubrics_metrics.name: Principle: combustion as oxygen absorption and product collection
rubrics_metrics.description: Combustion is decomposition (absorption) of oxygen gas by combustible substance with liberation of caloric and light; experiments must rigorously determine quantities of oxygen used and collect gaseous and condensed products.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Because combustion often produces gaseous products (CO2, N2 remains), apparatus must separate and measure gases and condense/absorb water and CO2 to allow quantitative accounting.

rubrics_metrics.name: Phosphorus/charcoal combustion in oxygen: apparatus and weighing protocol
rubrics_metrics.description: Use a gas-filled bell or evacuated balloon over mercury or pump to control atmosphere; place combusting material in a weighed porcelain capsule under the bell, ignite, then after combustion weigh to determine product mass (e.g., phosphoric acid).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Procedure specifics: fill bell with oxygen to brim, transfer over mercury, dry mercury surface, introduce capsule under bell (either by passing through mercury or briefly lifting bell), evacuate some gas to adjust mercury level before ignition (using siphon GHI or pump) to avoid expansion errors; ignite with red-hot iron or ignited tinder; after combustion allow to cool, delute and weigh. Also examine residual gas density for corrections.

rubrics_metrics.name: Avoid sample-size and placement precautions to prevent apparatus damage
rubrics_metrics.description: Do not burn too large a quantity of combustible in a finite gas volume: during initial expansion heat may push capsule upward; toward the end the capsule may approach dome and sudden high heat can fracture glass.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Ensure the sample size is small enough that the capsule does not approach the dome during combustion; monitor and control ignition initiation to avoid pressure spikes.

rubrics_metrics.name: Avoiding detonation with volatile combustibles
rubrics_metrics.description: Volatile substances (ether, alcohol, essential oils) dissolve in oxygen and can produce sudden detonation upon ignition that propels and shatters the bell.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Do not use the simple gas-bell ignition method for very volatile substances; adopt alternative apparatus and procedures that avoid explosive mixtures and allow complete collection of products (including condensed water).

rubrics_metrics.name: Balloon/closed-bottle method for phosphorus combustion to collect condensed products
rubrics_metrics.description: Use a large glass balloon with a fitted copper plate having two tubes; inside the balloon place a support and porcelain capsule with phosphorus, evacuate, admit oxygen from a gasometer, ignite, allow combustion to cease when acid phosphoric cloud forms, then delute and weigh balloon to obtain acid weight.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Weigh balloon+tare before and after; use pump to create vacuum before admitting oxygen; after combustion consider that the remaining gas may differ in density from air and correct calculations accordingly.

rubrics_metrics.name: Charcoal combustion furnace and gas-analysis setup
rubrics_metrics.description: A conical copper furnace with a grille and ash pan; charcoal introduced above a hollow ignition tube (RS) used to introduce a lit ember; air is supplied at controlled pressure by a gasometer via pipe lmn, and combustion effluent is passed through potash bottles to absorb CO2, leaving N2 which is measured in a receiving gasometer.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Determine weight of coal before and after, measure quantity of air introduced (gasometer), absorb CO2 in potash (increase in potash weight gives CO2 quantity), collect residual N2 for measuring volume and composition; immerse furnace in water/ice bath to moderate heat; use sight/glass mastiqué to confirm ignition.

rubrics_metrics.name: Quantitative accounting principles for solid combustion
rubrics_metrics.description: To obtain a complete analysis know: weight of combustible, volume of air used, amount/composition of remaining gas after combustion, weight of ash, and increase in potash bottles (CO2). From these derive proportions of carbon & oxygen in CO2 product.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Weigh all relevant elements precisely (charcoal, RS tube, ash, potash bottles). Combine gasometry and gravimetric absorption to determine component quantities.

rubrics_metrics.name: Combustion of oils: sealed bocal and comprehensive collection
rubrics_metrics.description: Burn oils in a sealed bocal with a mercury rigole seal and a lamp whose wick height can be externally adjusted; supply dry air from a gasometer, condense water through cooled serpentine and collect residual water in deliquescent tubes; pass remaining air through series of potash bottles to absorb CO2 and finally through limewater to verify complete CO2 removal.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Lamp and siphon details: set oil feed by screw/tube and siphon valves; divide combustion air around and through the wick (Argand-style) to improve combustion; condense water progressively in cooling coils and trap, then dry residual gas with deliquescent salt (tube 28–29) before measuring volume and sampling for O2/N2 ratio (sulfide of potassium test). Use many potash bottles (author recommends ~9) and check last with limewater for sensitivity.

rubrics_metrics.name: Collection and measurement of water produced in combustion of oils
rubrics_metrics.description: Condense water formed by combustion on cooled bocal walls and in a cooled serpentine, finish condensation in a receiver and absorb remaining vapor in a deliquescent salt tube to determine water quantity by weight.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Arrange cooling coils (serpentin) 17 & 18 immersed to condense progressively; weigh the tube + deliquescent salt before and after to determine absorbed water. Account for small product losses when assembling sealed bocal, and estimate them if necessary.

rubrics_metrics.name: Drying and final gas analysis after combustion
rubrics_metrics.description: After CO2 absorption pass the remaining gas through deliquescent salt to remove water, then collect in a gasometer to measure volume; take samples and assay residual O2 by sulfide of potassium or similar reagents to determine composition.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Correct gas volumes for barometer and thermometer as discussed in earlier chapters; use sensitive limewater at end of potash train to ensure no CO2 remains; account for any oxygen that escaped combustion when computing balances.

rubrics_metrics.name: Lamp wick management during oil combustion
rubrics_metrics.description: Maintain a precisely determined wick length: too long causes oil to vaporize more than air consumes and produces smoke; wick must be adjustable externally via a rod passing through a leather collar and gear/rack mechanism.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Adjust wick to an optimal length (three or four lines from edge in example); provide a delicate screw/pinion & rack to control without opening apparatus. Enclose flame with a small glass bocal to stabilize combustion and improve results.

rubrics_metrics.name: General experimental caution: patience, exactness, and avoiding disturbance
rubrics_metrics.description: Successful modern chemical experiments critically depend on careful lutting/sealing, patience, and precision; do not start experiments without testing seals and ensuring no movement—small disturbances destroy results.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Reiterate: never begin without trying seals, secure all parts, avoid jostling during sealing and tightening, and recognize that much of success depends on manipulation skill rather than solely on apparatus.
